<h3><b>Task 1

Q1. What is the medically relevant insight from the article?

A1. The paper presents a single-cell atlas of transcribed cis-regulatory elements (tCREs) across human tissues.
Key medical insight: Many disease-associated genetic variants are located in non-coding regions. Identifying cell-type-specific regulatory elements can help explain how these variants influence gene expression and contribute to complex diseases.
The atlas also shows that different cell types may use different regulatory elements to control the same gene, which may reveal disease mechanisms missed by gene-expression analysis alone.


Q2. Which genomics technology/ technologies were used?

A2. 
Single-cell 5′ RNA-seq: Main technology to identify transcription start sites and transcribed regulatory elements.
scATAC-seq: To examine chromatin accessibility.
Bulk RNA-seq and CAGE: To validate transcriptional activity and transcription start sites.
Promoter-capture Hi-C: To investigate interactions between distal regulatory elements and promoters.

Q3. List and explain at least three questions/ hypotheses you can think of that extend the analysis presented in the paper.

A3. 
・How do regulatory elements contribute to disease-associated genetic variants?
・How does cellular activation change regulatory-element activity?
・Do males and females have different regulatory mechanisms in disease-relevant cells?

3. What is the average and median CO2 uptake of the plants from Quebec and Mississippi?

```{r}
library(dplyr)
CO2 %>% 
  group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(mean_uptake = mean(uptake), median_uptake = median(uptake))
```

4. [Optional] In the “airway” example data from Bioconductor, how many genes are expressed in each sample? How many genes are not expressed in any sample?

```{r}
BiocManager::install("airway", ask = FALSE, update = TRUE)
library(airway)
data("airway")
Expression <- assay(airway) 
# Number of expressed genes (non-zero) per sample
expressed_per_sample <- colSums(Expression > 0)
# Number of genes not expressed in any sample
not_expressed <- sum(rowSums(Expression > 0) == 0)
#print
expressed_per_sample
not_expressed
```



<h3><b>Task 6

1. Write a function that calculates the ratio of the mean and the median of a given vector.
```{r}
mean_median_ratio <- function(x) {
  return(mean(x) / median(x))
}
```

2. Write a function that ignores the lowest and the highest value from a given vector and calculate the mean.

```{r}
mean_trimmed <- function(x) {
  x_sorted <- sort(x)
  return(mean(x_sorted[2:(length(x_sorted) - 1)]))
}
```

3. Read about piping from here:https://r4ds.had.co.nz/pipes.html#pipes ). Write a short (max. 300 characters, no spaces) explanation of why, how, and when not to use pipes.

A: Pipes make code clearer by chaining functions in order. Use them when applying multiple processes step by step. Avoid using them when logic is too complex.

4. Familiarize yourself with the apply-family of functions (apply, lapply, sapply etc.)
Write a short explanation (max. 300 characters, no spaces) of why they could be useful in your work.

A: Apply functions help replace explicit loops, making code shorter and faster. 
They are useful for applying a function across rows, columns, or list elements without writing repetitive for loops.

<h3><b>Task 7
1. Compare the distributions of the body heights of the two species from the 'magic_guys.csv' dataset graphically
a. using the basic 'hist' function as well as ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_histogram’ functions from the ggplot2 package. Optimize the plots for example by trying several different 'breaks'. Note that ggplot2-based functions give you many more options for changing the visualization parameters, try some of them.

A:
a-1 basic hist

```{r}
data <- read.csv("magic_guys.csv")
hist(data$length[data$species == "jedi"], 
     breaks = 20, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),
     xlim = range(data$length), main = "Height Distribution",
     xlab = "Height")
```

```{r}
hist(data$length[data$species == "sith"], 
     breaks = 20, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),
     xlim = range(data$length), main = "Height Distribution",
     xlab = "Height")
```

```{r}
# different "break" value
hist(data$length[data$species == "jedi"], 
     breaks = 10, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),
     xlim = range(data$length), main = "Height Distribution",
     xlab = "Height")
```

```{r}
hist(data$length[data$species == "sith"], 
     breaks = 10, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),
     xlim = range(data$length), main = "Height Distribution",
     xlab = "Height")
```

  a-2-1 ggplot
  
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data, aes(x = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 20) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Height Distribution by Species")
```
  
  a-2-2 ggplot parameter changing
  
```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 15) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Height Distribution by Species (bins = 15)")
```  

b. Do the same comparison as in a. but with boxplots. If you want to use the ggplot2-package, use the functions ‘ggplot’ and ‘geom_boxplot’.

A:
b-1 basic R

```{r}
boxplot(length ~ species, data = data, col = c("lightpink", "lightblue"),
        main = "Boxplot of Heights", ylab = "Height")
```

b-2 ggplot

```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = species, y = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Heights")
```


c. Save the plots with the ‘png’, ‘pdf’, and ‘svg’ formats. In which situation would you use which file format?

```{r}
png("boxplot.png"); print(
  ggplot(data, aes(x = species, y = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Heights"));
#  dev.off()
```

```{r}
pdf("boxplot.pdf"); print(
  ggplot(data, aes(x = species, y = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Heights"));
#  dev.off()
```

```{r}
svg("boxplot.svg"); print(
  ggplot(data, aes(x = species, y = length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Heights"));
#  dev.off()
```

PNG → good for quick viewing, slides, or raster images.

PDF → vector graphics, best for publications.

SVG → scalable web graphics, useful for editing in Illustrator or Inkscape.



2. Load the gene expression data matrix from the ‘microarray_data.tab’ dataset provided in the shared folder, it is a big tabular separated matrix.
a. How big is the matrix in terms of rows and columns?

A:
553 rows and 1000 columns.

```{r}
microarray <- read.table("microarray_data.tab", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")
# Dimensions
dim(microarray)
```
b. Count the missing values per gene and visualize this result.

A:
b-1

```{r}
missing_counts <- rowSums(is.na(microarray))
hist(missing_counts, main = "Missing values per gene", xlab = "Missing values")
```
b-2

```{r}
names(missing_counts) <- paste0("Gene", seq_along(missing_counts))
barplot(missing_counts,
        names.arg = names(missing_counts),   #  gene num
        las = 2,                      
        cex.names = 0.6,              # font size
        main = "Missing values per gene",
        xlab = "Gene index",
        ylab = "Missing values",
        col = "grey30",
        border = NA)
```



c. Find the genes for which there are more than X% (X=10%, 20%, 50%) missing values.

A:
c-1

```{r}
genes_missing <- function(x) {
  n_samples <- ncol(microarray)
  return (which(missing_counts > x / 100 * n_samples))
}
genes_missing(10)
```
c-2

```{r}
genes_missing(20)
```

c-3

```{r}
genes_missing(50)
```

d. Replace the missing values by the average expression value for the particular gene. (Note: Imputing data has to be used with caution!)
A:

```{r}
microarray_imputed <- microarray
row_means <- rowMeans(microarray, na.rm = TRUE)
for (i in 1:nrow(microarray_imputed)) {
  microarray_imputed[i, is.na(microarray_imputed[i, ])] <- row_means[i]
}
# test
missing_counts_2 <- rowSums(is.na(microarray_imputed))
missing_counts_2
```


3. Visualize the data in the CO2 dataset in a way that gives you a deeper understanding of the data. What do you see?
A:
Plants from Quebec and Mississippi respond differently to CO2 concentration.
Treatment (chilled vs nonchilled) also influences uptake.

```{r}
# Scatter plot of uptake vs concentration by Type and Treatment
ggplot(CO2, aes(x = conc, y = uptake, color = Type, shape = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "CO2 Uptake vs Concentration",
       x = "CO2 concentration",
       y = "Uptake")
```

Installation

a. Extract summary statistics (mean, median and maximum) for the following variables from the ‘chromosome’ data: variations, protein coding genes, and miRNAs. Utilize the tidyverse functions to make this as simply as possible.

A:

```{r}
c <- chromosome %>%
  summarise(
    mean_variations = mean(variations, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_variations = median(variations, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_variations = max(variations, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_protein_coding = mean(protein_codinggenes, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_protein_coding = median(protein_codinggenes, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_protein_coding = max(protein_codinggenes, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_miRNAs = mean(mi_rna, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_miRNAs = median(mi_rna, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_miRNAs = max(mi_rna, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
c
```

b. How does the chromosome size distribute? Plot a graph that helps to visualize this by using ggplot2 package functions.

A:

```{r}
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x = basepairs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Chromosome Size", x = "Chromosome Size (bp)", y = "Count")
```

or

```{r}
# or
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x = id, y = basepairs)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Chromosome Size (bp)",
    x = "Chromosome",
    y = "Size (bp)"
  )
```

c. Does the number of protein coding genes or miRNAs correlate with the length of the chromosome? Make two separate plots to visualize these relationships.

A:
c-1 protein coding gene

```{r}
# Protein coding genes vs chromosome length
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x = basepairs, y = protein_codinggenes)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "darkred") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Correlation between Chromosome size and Protein coding genes",
       x = "Chromosome Size (bp)", y = "Number of Protein Coding Genes")
```

c-2 miRNAs

```{r}
# miRNAs vs chromosome length
ggplot(chromosome, aes(x = basepairs, y = mi_rna)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "darkred") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Correlation between Chromosome size and miRNAs",
       x = "Chromosome Size (bp)", y = "Number of miRNAs")
```

d. Calculate the same summary statistics for the ‘proteins’ data variables length and mass. Create a meaningful visualization of the relationship between these two variables by utilizing the ggplot2 package functions. Play with the colors, theme- and other visualization parameters to create a plot that pleases you.

A:
d-1

```{r}
# Summary statistics
p <- proteins %>%
  summarise(
    mean_length = mean(length, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_length = median(length, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_length = max(length, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_mass = mean(mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_mass = median(mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_mass = max(mass, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
p
```

d-2

```{r}
# Scatter plot of length vs mass
ggplot(proteins, aes(x = length, y = mass)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "darkred") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Correlation between Protein Length and Mass",
       x = "Protein Length (aa)", y = "Protein Mass (kDa)")
```
